claims.statement: On January 16, 1893, the United States Minister and naval representatives caused armed naval forces of the United States to invade the sovereign Hawaiian nation and position themselves near ʻIolani Palace to intimidate the Queen and her government; on January 17 the kingdom was overthrown, and to avoid bloodshed she yielded her authority, under protest, to the United States rather than to the Provisional Government.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The historical trauma that the modern episode acknowledges; recorded as history, not as a symptom. Wording follows the 1993 Apology Resolution.

Her memoir captions a picture of the palace: "My palace was my prison."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded as history, plainly and without dramatization; not a medical event.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: A minor ischemic stroke presenting as a transient ischemic attack in a 78-year-old Native Hawaiian elder, composer and community leader in Honolulu. The episode covers same-day evaluation of transient weakness and speech difficulty (ABCD2 score, CT and CT angiography of the head and neck, then diffusion MRI the next morning, which turns a suspected TIA into a minor stroke); a 21-day course of aspirin and clopidogrel started within 24 hours, as in POINT and CHANCE; ECG, echocardiogram and 30-day rhythm monitoring that find paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, and the change from antiplatelets to apixaban with correct dosing; a high-intensity statin to an LDL below 70 mg/dL; a blood pressure target below 130/80 mmHg; swallow, cognition, mood and falls screening; a nosebleed on apixaban; all under the 1912 AHA/ASA secondary stroke prevention guideline and the CMID stroke and atrial fibrillation monographs. It also teaches culturally safe care: asking how she wishes to be addressed, involving her ʻohana as she chooses, offering Native Hawaiian healing such as lomilomi and hoʻoponopono alongside Western care without probing or describing practices, and acknowledging the historical trauma of the overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom, which the United States formally apologized for in 1884.

hpi.narrative: Liliʻuokalani, a 78-year-old woman who had a minor ischemic stroke two months ago and takes apixaban for paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, came the same day with a nosebleed. This morning, after blowing her nose, the left nostril bled steadily for about 15 minutes; it stopped when a member of her ʻohana had her sit forward and pinch the soft part of her nose for ten minutes, as the clinic's handout showed. She did not swallow much blood or vomit. The air in her bedroom has been dry from a fan running all night, and her nose has felt crusted for a week. This is her first nosebleed in years. She has had no other bleeding: no bruising, blood in the urine, black stools or bleeding gums. She takes apixaban twice daily and has not missed a dose, and she has taken no aspirin, ibuprofen or naproxen. She has had no new weakness, numbness or speech trouble.

assessment.assessment: By the tissue-based definition this was a minor ischemic stroke, not a transient ischemic attack: the symptoms resolved, but the MRI shows an infarct in the hand area of the left motor cortex. A single small cortical infarct is embolic in pattern. The likeliest sources are the heart, particularly atrial fibrillation, given her age and a mildly enlarged left atrium, and less likely the left carotid plaque, which narrows the artery by less than 50%. Until a source is found, this is an embolic stroke of undetermined source

Yes. For a minor noncardioembolic stroke or high-risk TIA, aspirin with clopidogrel started within 24 hours and given for 21 days lowers early recurrence (CHANCE, POINT); hers was started at about 18 hours. Bleeding risk rises if it is continued longer, so after 21 days she should take a single antiplatelet, clopidogrel, unless atrial fibrillation is found

An embolic-appearing stroke at 78 warrants at least 30 days of ambulatory monitoring; a 30-day patch was applied today. If atrial fibrillation is found, stop the antiplatelet and start a direct oral anticoagulant: apixaban 5 mg twice daily, since she meets only one dose-reduction criterion (weight 60 kg or less). Less than 50% narrowing does not warrant endarterectomy or stenting; treatment is a statin, blood pressure control and her antithrombotic. No follow-up carotid imaging is needed unless new symptoms arise
